## claude.ai Dropbox
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- add-backlinks: Add backlinks from related blog posts and glossary entries to a target post. Use when the user wants to improve internal linking by having other content link back to a specific article.
- blog-post: Create or revise a blog post for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to write a new blog post, revise/refresh an existing one, or update content. Guides through gathering information, content structure, internal linking, and post-publish steps.
- evergreen-posting: Generate a batch of evergreen social media posts (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky) promoting the AI Failure Modes quiz and existing blog posts / glossary entries. Use when Mark says "create posts", "schedule social media", "draft an evergreen batch", or asks for N days of social content. Outputs a single JSON file the posting pipeline can consume, and marks the source calendars so the same content isn't promoted twice.
- glossary-entry: Create a new glossary term for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to add a new Agile/Scrum term definition, concept explanation, or methodology entry to the glossary.
- indexing-strategy: Use this skill when Mark asks to analyze, plan, or implement SEO topic clusters and internal linking for agilepainrelief.com. Covers two modes: (1) ANALYZE mode — audit existing content, identify pillar/cluster opportunities, find gaps and orphaned pages, and produce a prioritized action plan; (2) IMPLEMENT mode — generate specific internal linking instructions, write or revise blog posts and glossary entries to fit the cluster strategy, and produce per-page checklists. Also use when Mark asks what a blog post or glossary entry needs for SEO, or when he wants to check whether a draft meets the cluster linking requirements.
- newsletter: Draft and send a newsletter to the Newsletter Subscribers list via Cakemail, starting from plain markdown. Use when Mark wants to write, render, test, or dispatch a newsletter / email campaign, or turn a markdown file into a Cakemail draft campaign. Drives the email-automation CLI's send-newsletter command.
- social-media-adapt: Adapt LinkedIn posts to Mastodon and Bluesky formats with platform-specific character limits, thread formatting, and JSON structure. Use when Claude needs to convert LinkedIn content to other social platforms, create threaded posts, or adapt content for different character limits (Mastodon 500 chars, Bluesky 290 chars).
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. - claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

## 2026-07-16 — Astro 6 → 7 upgrade

**Why.** Staying current with the framework. `npx @astrojs/upgrade` aborted with
"Dependencies failed to install," and the failure cascaded through several layers,
each hidden behind the last.

**What we did.**
- **Cause 1 — the release-age gate.** `.npmrc` carries `min-release-age=7` (supply-chain
  hardening). `astro@7.1.0` was published the same day and `@astrojs/mdx@7.0.3` /
  `@astrojs/netlify@8.1.2` three days prior, so npm had no version old enough to satisfy
  the rule and gave up. Ran the upgrade install once with `--min-release-age=0`; the
  checked-in `.npmrc` is unchanged (the gate still applies to normal installs).
- **Cause 2 — in-place ERESOLVE.** `npm i pkg@new` tries to mutate the existing tree in
  place, which can't cleanly swap a whole framework major. Switched to a clean install
  (delete `node_modules` + lockfile, edit `package.json` to the targets, reinstall).
- **Cause 3 — two stale `overrides`.** `@astrojs/markdown-remark: 7.2.0` was a dead
  astro-6/mdx-5 workaround. `vite: "^7"` was the real build-breaker: astro 7 depends on
  **vite ^8**, and the override force-pinned vite 7, producing the cryptic
  `rollupOptions.input should not be an html file when building for SSR`. Removed the
  whole `overrides` block.
- **Cause 4 — latent malformed markup.** `src/components/courses/course-preview.astro`
  had an unclosed `container` div. Astro 6's lenient compiler auto-recovered and rendered
  it fine; astro 7's stricter compiler errors on it. Closed the tag. Going forward
  `astro build` (which Netlify runs on every deploy) catches this class of error, so a
  malformed template now fails the build instead of shipping.
- **Ecosystem bumps + config migration.** `astro-embed`→0.13.1 and `astro-og-canvas`→0.13.0
  (their astro-7-compatible releases, clearing the peer warnings). Migrated
  `astro.config.mjs` markdown plugins off the now-deprecated `markdown.remarkPlugins` /
  `rehypePlugins` onto `markdown.processor: unified({...})` from `@astrojs/markdown-remark`,
  so the build is warning-free. `astro check` and the production build are both clean.

## 2026-06-19 — Bot-proofing the newsletter / quiz signups

**The problem.** Cakemail was filling up with junk contacts: random gibberish
names, no tags, some auto-confirmed (corporate email security scanners click the
double-opt-in link automatically). They were bots POSTing straight to our Cakemail
hosted-form URLs, which were sitting in the public page JavaScript for anyone to
scrape. A "tick here if you're not human" honeypot didn't help, because a bot
POSTing directly to Cakemail never loads our form, so it never sees the honeypot.

**What we learned.**
- A client-side guard can't stop a direct POST. The protection has to sit on the
  server, in front of the thing being abused.
- reCAPTCHA v3 isn't really "deprecated", but Google now forces you through a Cloud
  project to get a key. We chose **Cloudflare Turnstile** instead: free, static
  keys that never rotate, no Google account. (Rotating keys was exactly the pain
  that made us delete the previous server function, so "set and forget" mattered.)
- The earlier server function hurt because of Cakemail's auto-rotating OAuth token.
  The new function needs **no Cakemail credentials at all** — the hosted form
  accepts anonymous POSTs, so the function just checks the Turnstile token and
  forwards. Nothing to rotate.

**What we did.**
- Added one Netlify function, `/api/newsletter-signup`. Every signup (newsletter
  form, both AI lead-magnet forms, and the quiz) now POSTs there with a Turnstile
  token; the function verifies the token, then forwards to Cakemail server-side.
- Moved the Cakemail form URL out of the browser bundle into a server-only file,
  and consolidated everything onto one Cakemail form (tags do the segmentation).
  Bots can no longer scrape the URL from the page.
- Gated the quiz too, without polluting the (deliberately reusable) quiz engine:
  added two generic hooks to the engine (`onSubmit` + a widget slot) and put all
  the APR/Turnstile specifics in a small wrapper.
- Removed the old honeypot from the three signup forms (Turnstile replaces it).
  The contact form keeps its honeypot — it's a separate Formspree form, not behind
  Turnstile.

**Still manual:** the public Turnstile site key is a constant in the repo; the
secret is set in Netlify (`TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY`). Old Cakemail forms get deleted
once a test signup confirms the new one works.

## 2026-01-21 — Native markdown footnotes (dropped the custom components)

**The problem.** Footnotes used custom Astro components (`footnotes.astro` /
`footnotes-simple.astro`), so every post had to import a component and wrap its
footnote definitions in JSX — cumbersome next to plain markdown syntax.

**What we did.** Switched to **remark-gfm** for native GFM footnotes (`[^1]` inline,
`[^1]: …` at the bottom, no imports), plus a small custom rehype plugin
(`src/utils/plugins/rehypeFootnoteLinks.ts`).

**The one non-obvious decision — scroll-to-top.** By default remark-gfm links each
reference to its specific definition (`#user-content-fn-1`). Two problems: the
sticky header covered the target, and jumping mid-list felt disorienting. So the
plugin rewrites every footnote reference to point at `#footnotes` (the top of the
section) and adds `id="footnotes"` to the generated `<section>`; `global.css` then
only needs one `scroll-margin-top: 6rem` offset rule. More predictable for readers,
one offset to maintain. (The deprecated `<Footnotes>` component path is gone — see
CLAUDE.md "Footnotes".)
